clue.text: In the mountains a flapper may be sorely a-tramping

indicators.note: sorely suggests the letters are battered and hurt out of shape, so the hiking phrase is rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird of the high peaks is pictured trudging along with aching feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorely' signals rearranging the nine letters of A-TRAMPING. 'A flapper' is a bird, not a 1920s girl, and this one lives on mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird in question is a grouse of high mountain slopes, and any bird is something that flaps its wings.

clue.text: Watch or spy on everything across the Channel

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a watch on everything happening over in France.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing tipster who spies on horses at training is a tout; and across the Channel, in French, the word for everything is tout.

clue.text: Rode wildly round a thoroughfare and got hauled over the coals

indicators.note: round says the rearranged letters go around the other pieces
riding wildly suggests the letters of the word are thrown about in a new order

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a thoroughfare

explanation.surface: Someone rides recklessly round a road and gets a severe telling-off for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' rearranges RODE to ROED, and 'round' puts A plus ST inside it after RO.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hauled over the coals is an idiom for a harsh scolding, and being roasted is the same idiom of heat-as-criticism.

clue.text: Live in with one of 8?

parts.note: 8-across is REGULAR HABITS, so one of them is a single habit

explanation.surface: Someone moves in alongside a creature of routine.
explanation.walkthrough: '8' points to the 8-across answer; one of its habits supplies the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To live somewhere is to dwell in or occupy it, which is the verb's sense.

clue.text: Where early Christians read from quondam books

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: The early Church read aloud from books of former times.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across the join of 'quondAM BOoks'. 'quondam' means former, and looks like it should mean something.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a raised reading desk or pulpit in early churches, from which scripture lessons were read.

clue.text: Nobody knew the secret of this fine mushroom crop

definitions.text: Nobody knew the secret of this fine mushroom crop

parts.words: Nobody knew the secret of this fine mushroom crop
parts.note: mushrooms are grown without light, and a person nobody tells a secret to is also left unlit, so to speak

explanation.surface: A grower's prize crop of mushrooms came from a method no one else knew.
explanation.definitionFit: Being uninformed is the idiomatic sense, and mushrooms are literally grown away from light.

clue.text: If an untrained pilot is here we wouldn't be flying by George!

definitions.text: If an untrained pilot is here we wouldn't be flying by George!

parts.words: If an untrained pilot is here we wouldn't be flying by George!
parts.note: George is airmen's slang for the autopilot, so flying by George means on autopilot, not a mild oath

explanation.surface: A passenger exclaims they would not fly if a novice were in the cockpit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' reads as an old exclamation, but George is the RAF nickname for an aircraft's automatic pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in charge of steering, at the cockpit levers and stick.

clue.text: Customs gone through like clockwork with army outfits

parts.note: the regular army is the standing professional force, so army stands for regular
habits are outfits, as a nun's or rider's dress

explanation.surface: Soldiers' uniforms pass through customs inspection without a hitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customs' looks like the border authority, but it means routines.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs here are routines, and doing them like clockwork makes them steady, repeated practices.

clue.text: It is ground where games are finely balanced

definitions.text: It is ground where games are finely balanced

parts.words: It is ground where games are finely balanced
parts.note: a blade's sharp side is ground on a stone, and a closely matched contest is said to be poised on it

explanation.surface: This sounds like a sports field where every match is evenly contested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like a playing field but is the past tense of grind, as in sharpening.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharpened side of a blade is literally ground, and the phrase also describes a precarious, evenly poised situation.

clue.text: Conveniently organised port open

indicators.note: organised suggests the letters are put into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the words as printed, which lack the U the answer also needs

explanation.surface: A harbour is opened up efficiently and in an orderly way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' rearranges the fodder, but PORT OPEN has only eight letters and lacks the U the nine-letter answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Something conveniently timed is well suited to the moment, the adverb sense standing for the adjective.

clue.text: Cracked coal in little lumps

explanation.surface: A bag of coal has been broken into small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracked is slang for crazy, which nuts also means; and small lumps of coal are sold under that name.

clue.text: Wounds night fliers going back to a point

indicators.note: going back says the creatures' name is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: bats are creatures that fly by night
S is south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Bats returning to roost at a certain spot inflict injuries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going back' turns BATS into STAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Stabs are knife wounds, so the plural noun matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Talk about business! That's where it's done!

explanation.surface: Someone urges discussion of trade, then points to the place it happens.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk about one's work is to talk shop, so the word alone is used as the verb; and a store is where business is carried on.

clue.text: Diana and Vivienne briefly upset 19

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the pieces are turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: Di is the short form of the name Diana
Viv is the short form of the name Vivienne

explanation.surface: Two women, Diana and Vivienne, are upset by something graphic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns DIVIV around. '19' refers to the answer at 19-down, GRAPHIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Vivid and graphic both describe a description so lifelike it can be pictured.

clue.text: Stop launch and rock royal boat

indicators.note: to rock a boat is to shake it about, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A royal boat is set rocking just as it is about to be launched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' signals rearranging R and BOAT. 'launch' looks like a boat but is the launch of a mission.
explanation.definitionFit: To call off a launch is to cancel a mission or flight before it is completed.

clue.text: Imagined to be highly favoured?

explanation.surface: Someone only supposed they were the favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to suppose it; and a horse fancied by punters is strongly backed.

clue.text: One of Raleigh's weedier transplants

parts.note: Sir Walter Raleigh is credited with bringing a plant from the Americas to England, and it is nicknamed the weed

explanation.surface: This sounds like a weak seedling moved by an Elizabethan gardener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weedier' looks like puny, but the plant is called 'the weed'. Raleigh popularised smoking in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The smoking leaf was one of the New World plants brought across to England and grown there.

clue.text: Throwing back some speech uttered in high places?

definitions.text: Throwing back some speech uttered in high places?

parts.words: Throwing back some speech uttered in high places?
parts.note: words shouted in the mountains are thrown back by the rock faces

explanation.surface: This sounds like politicians in power repeating someone's speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high places' suggests people in power, but here they are mountains, where a shout comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound reflected back from cliffs is repeated, which is what the participle describes.

clue.text: An illustration of lifelike quality

explanation.surface: A picture is praised for its realism.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture or diagram in print is called that noun; and a vivid, realistic description is that adjective.

clue.text: The lowest calling a Briton can inherit

definitions.text: The lowest calling a Briton can inherit

parts.words: The lowest calling a Briton can inherit
parts.note: calling means rank, and the bottom hereditary title in Britain is meant, below baron but above knight

explanation.surface: This sounds like the humblest job a British person could be born into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calling' looks like a trade or vocation, but it is a title; this one ranks lowest among hereditary honours.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lowest hereditary rank in the British honours system, passed down to an heir.

clue.text: On the verge of tears when the water couldn't rise higher!

definitions.text: when the water couldn't rise higher!

explanation.surface: Someone close to crying, like a tank about to overflow.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes about to spill tears are full to the edge; and a vessel filled to its rim is the same.

clue.text: Gallery idols

explanation.surface: Worshipped images on display in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British theatre the cheapest seats at the very top are called 'the gods'.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest balcony in a theatre is nicknamed this; and idols are false deities.

clue.text: The arty scholar's put in to bowl

parts.note: a BA, a Bachelor of Arts, is an arty scholar, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: An arts graduate is sent in to bowl in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bowl' looks like a cricket action but is the vessel. BA is a Bachelor of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A basin is a round open dish or wash bowl.

clue.text: We get involved with the Navy and so did she

indicators.note: to get involved is to become tangled up, so these letters are mixed together

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: We join up with the Navy, and so did she.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get involved' mixes WE with RN, the Royal Navy. 'so did she' defines: a woman who joined the Women's Royal Naval Service was called a Wren.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Women's Royal Naval Service was a woman who joined up with the Navy.

clue.text: Tailless llama going up to Buck House

indicators.note: going up in a down clue means the letters read from bottom to top
tailless says the animal loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A llama without a tail climbs towards Buckingham Palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailless' cuts LLAMA to LLAM, and 'going up' turns it round. Buck House is Buckingham Palace, at the end of the London avenue this names.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mall is the ceremonial London road leading straight to Buckingham Palace.

clue.text: Consort with the greatest of Greek 2

definitions.text: Consort with the greatest of Greek

parts.words: Consort with the greatest of Greek
parts.note: the wife of Zeus, chief of the Olympian deities, is meant

explanation.surface: Someone keeps company with the finest of the Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue means 'Greek 21', 21-across being GODS: she was wife of Zeus, the greatest of the Greek gods.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the queen of Olympus and wife to Zeus, king of the deities.

clue.text: Relax! They're not taxing the air

explanation.surface: An order to unwind, followed by news that no levy is charged on air.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe easily is to stop worrying; and if air is not taxed, one may inhale without charge.

clue.text: First play of spade or club can be negated by new rubber

definitions.text: First play of spade or club can be negated by new rubber

parts.words: First play of spade or club can be negated by new rubber
parts.note: leading a spade or club is leading a dark suit at bridge, and pencil graphite marks are removed by an eraser, also called a rubber

explanation.surface: A bridge player's opening card is cancelled when a new rubber begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubber' looks like a set of bridge games but is an eraser, which removes graphite.
explanation.definitionFit: Graphite, used in pencils and for polishing grates, goes by this name, and its pencil marks can be rubbed out.
